title: Kichaka, and the order of the aims
hookLine: Kichaka puts desire above dharma, and the Kama Sutra ranks the aims for a clash.
carry: in a clash: dharma, then artha, then kama
tomorrow: a wife is told her husband has a year to live. what does she do?
last: A RIGHTFUL AIM, IN ITS FITTING PLACE.

lines: A COMMANDER WANTS WHAT ISN'T HIS.
cards: In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas spend a year in hiding at King Virata's court, and Draupadi serves the queen in disguise. The queen's brother Kichaka commands the army, and he wants Draupadi.
She refuses him, again and again. He won't take no. He presses, he threatens, and he strikes her in the king's own hall, sure his power puts him above the rule.
That night Draupadi goes to Bhima. The next evening Kichaka comes to the dance hall expecting her, and finds Bhima instead. By morning the commander is dead.

teach.h: KICHAKA, RUINED BY KAMA GONE WRONG.
teach.b: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter names Kichaka too, with Ravana and others, as men ruined by kama gone wrong. That's striking in a book named for kama.
And the chapter sets a rule for when the three aims pull against each other. The earlier, Vatsyayana says, outweighs the later.
Dharma over artha. Artha over kama. So a book named for pleasure, in its own ethics chapter, puts pleasure third.

teach.h: A RULE FOR A CLASH, NOT A BAN.
teach.b: It's a rule for a clash, not an order to drop the later aims; the same chapter gives kama its own place. And the ladder bends by role.
For a king, Vatsyayana says, artha should come first, because people's livelihood depends on it, the Arthashastra's verdict back again, but only for the job of ruling.
Kichaka had power and wealth, and let desire rule both, against a woman's no. That's the order turned upside down.
One way to bring it home: when you can't have all three, start with what's right, like a promise; then what keeps you going, like a shift; then what you enjoy.

how: Hindu teachers often explain the purusharthas, the aims of life, as a balance in which dharma guides the others; the Kama Sutra's opening sets out their order in a conflict, and the Mahabharata's Kichaka is a classic picture of the order reversed.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: the part of a well-known old book that ranks pleasure over all else
the part of a well-known old book that orders life's aims in a clash
the part of a well-known old book that bans pleasure altogether

games.q: when the aims collide — tap the pairs.
p: puts artha first: livelihoods depend on it

s: given its name, the Kama Sutra ranks pleasure first
in a clash, its ethics chapter puts dharma first, then artha, then kama.
the chapter makes an exception for a king: artha first
because people's livelihood depends on it, the same verdict the Arthashastra gave.
the ranking means the later aims should be given up
it's a rule for when they collide; the same chapter gives kama its own place.

games.q: your friend is treasurer of a club and holds everyone's trip money. a fun outing she's excited about falls on the deadline to pay the bus company. by the chapter's ranking, what comes first?
o: the outing. kama is a real aim, and she's earned it.
paying the bus, since everyone's trip depends on it.
skip both. when aims clash, it's safest to do neither.
games.why: in a clash the chapter puts artha above kama, and it bends the order further when others' livelihood depends on your work. the outing isn't wrong; it's later.

practice: Think of one clash coming up in your own week: two things wanting the same hour. Hindus begin a puja or a vow with a sankalpa, a short spoken resolve.

Make one now: name the higher aim you'll honor first, and one small step that keeps the other without throwing it away. If you pray, say it quietly to God or before your family's shrine. If you don't, say it once to yourself.
Then breathe slowly, and let it settle.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: when the aims collide, dharma, then artha, then kama, with artha first for a king.

orig.note: Sanskrit trivarga, the group of three: dharma, artha and kama.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: in a clash, dharma, then artha, then kama. Even pleasure's own book puts pleasure third. Day fifteen ninety-four.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Kichaka pursues Draupadi, disguised as the queen's maid, strikes her in the court, and is killed by Bhima in the dance hall)
Kama Sutra 1.2 (the trivarga; each earlier aim weightier than the later; artha first for a king; Kichaka and Ravana named among those ruined by kama)
Arthashastra 1.7 (artha is chief; points back to day 1591)
